title: Data platform migration plan
scratchpad:
Fernhollow, NOT Quarrystone (backups in Canada unless enterprise)
43k/yr on 2yr commit (list 52k)
cutover Mon Jan 11 (not Nov 30 - year-end close)
parallel run 4 wks from Dec 14
Brindle off Fri Jan 29, renews Feb 15
3 yrs history, rest archived; dashboard every 15 min
Greta: finance reports by Dec 18
segments: Okay, let's get started. This is the data platform plan. I want to leave with a vendor, a date and owners, in roughly that order.
Sounds good. I sent a pre-read last night, but I'll go through it quickly, since I know nobody reads pre-reads the night before.
I read it at breakfast, so you're half right. I'm here mostly for the cost section and the dates, to be honest.
Fair. Quick recap of where we are. All our reporting runs off Brindle, the hosted warehouse we signed with three years ago.
Every night a batch job copies the production database into Brindle, and every report, the finance ones and the customer ones, reads from that copy.
Which means every number anyone looks at is at least a day old. For finance that's fine. For dispatchers it's useless.
The dispatcher dashboard Marcus is speccing wants today's numbers, not yesterday's. Jobs completed so far today, who's running late, that kind of thing.
And the commercial side: Brindle renews on the fifteenth of February. If we're still on it then, that's another full year at sixty one thousand dollars.
Which is the part I care about. Sixty one thousand for a nightly copy is a lot of money for what we get out of it.
So the goals are fresher data for the dashboard, a lower bill, and being off Brindle before the fifteenth of February. Anything else?
Row-level access. We want customers to export their own reports eventually, which means the warehouse has to guarantee each customer only ever sees their own rows.
That one matters a lot. A customer seeing another customer's jobs in an export would be the worst bug we could possibly ship.
Okay, that's four goals: fresher data, a lower bill, off Brindle before February, and row-level access. Anselm, vendors.
I looked at five and cut it down to two. Quarrystone and Fernhollow. Both do streaming ingestion, so we'd stop copying everything nightly.
The other three weren't close. Two were basically the same product as Brindle with a new logo, and one wanted us to run the servers ourselves.
Running it ourselves is a firm no from me. We'd end up on call for a database none of us built, at three in the morning.
Quarrystone is the cheaper one by a distance. For our data volume, my estimate is about thirty four thousand dollars a year.
Fernhollow's list price for the same volume is fifty two thousand a year. Their tooling is nicer, but it's a lot more money.
Thirty four against fifty two. Unless Fernhollow does something Quarrystone can't, I know which one I'd pick.
Does Quarrystone do the row-level access I mentioned? That's the one thing I'd want to check before we pick anything.
Their docs say yes. I haven't tested it myself. I've got a trial account and I've been loading some anonymised job data into it this week.
What about getting data in? Streaming means something reads our database's change log continuously. That's load on production.
Both read the change log from the replica, not the primary. So production writes aren't touched. The replica does a bit more work.
The replica already struggles on Monday mornings when everyone runs their weekly reports. I'd want numbers before I believe a bit more work.
Okay. Tentatively, Quarrystone, on price, pending Anselm's trial. Let's do the timeline next, since that's where the Brindle date bites.
My plan was a two week parallel run, both warehouses fed at the same time, then cut over on Monday the thirtieth of November.
That leaves December and January as slack before the Brindle renewal, which felt comfortably safe to me.
Can I stop you there? The thirtieth of November is a problem for me. Our year-end close runs through December, and every close report reads from Brindle.
I'm not switching the source of the revenue numbers in the middle of year-end close. If anything doesn't match, I'll have no idea which side is wrong.
That's a fair point. Finance reports are the ones where a rounding difference turns into a week of reconciliation.
So after the close, then? When is the close actually done?
The books are closed in the first week of January. After that I don't care what you switch, as long as January's numbers match.
Then the first Monday after the close is the eleventh. That's still more than a month before the Brindle renewal.
Okay. The cutover moves from the thirtieth of November to Monday the eleventh of January, after year-end close is done.
And the parallel run? Two weeks feels short to me. I'd want it to cover a month end, so we can compare the monthly reports line by line.
If we cut over on the eleventh, a month end in the parallel run means starting in the middle of December.
Then make it four weeks. Parallel run from Monday the fourteenth of December, so December's month end is inside it, and cut over on the eleventh.
That I like. December's numbers come out of both systems, and I can check them against each other before anything switches.
Four weeks of feeding both means four weeks of double load on the replica, over the holidays, when nobody's around to watch it.
The Brindle side is the nightly copy we already run, so nothing changes there. It's only the new stream that's extra.
Okay. Then I'd like an alert on replica lag before the parallel run starts, not after something goes wrong.
Fine, that's a condition. And while we're on the parallel run, how do we decide it passed? I don't want four weeks of comparing and then an argument.
For finance, close enough is not a phrase I use. Revenue totals have to match to the cent, every single day of the run.
Row counts per table per day, plus the revenue totals Greta mentioned. I'll write a comparison job that runs every morning and posts the differences.
And for the dashboard, jobs completed per day per customer. If those drift, the dispatchers will notice long before we do.
What happens if the numbers don't match? Do we stop the run, or keep going and investigate on the side?
Keep going and investigate on the side. Stopping resets the clock, and we'd lose the December month end, which is the whole point of four weeks.
Agreed. The run keeps going, any mismatch gets a ticket the same day, and the cutover only happens if the last full week matches.
Next, history. Anselm, how much are we moving?
My plan was all of it. Six years of job history, every job, every status change, every invoice line.
Do we actually need six years in the warehouse? I checked last month, and no report we have looks back more than three.
The only thing that ever touches older data is the occasional customer asking for an export of their whole history, and that's rare.
Finance needs seven years kept somewhere, for tax. But kept somewhere doesn't mean kept in the expensive warehouse.
Old data in Fernhollow or Quarrystone costs the same per gigabyte as new data. Archive files in cold storage cost almost nothing.
Then three years goes into the new warehouse, and anything older goes to archive files in cold storage. If a customer wants their full history, we restore it.
As long as the archive files are kept for the full seven years, I'm happy with that.
That also cuts the backfill time a lot. Three years should load in a weekend instead of a week.
And restoring from the archive should be a script we test once, not something we figure out the first time a customer asks for it.
Good. Freshness next, which is really the whole reason we're doing this. Mirela, what does the dashboard actually need?
Before Mirela answers, my default was hourly. Hourly loads are cheap, they're easy to monitor, and they're a big step up from nightly.
Hourly is too slow for dispatchers. If someone's running late, they need to know within minutes. I'd want every five minutes.
Every five minutes for every table is a lot of extra work on the replica. Most of those tables don't change that often anyway.
Can we split it? The handful of tables the dashboard reads get refreshed often, and everything else stays nightly.
That works for me. The dashboard only needs jobs, job status changes and technician check-ins.
Then every fifteen minutes for those. Five minutes I'd have to test properly, and I don't want to promise it before we've measured the replica.
Fifteen minutes is fine for a first version. Dispatchers will take that over day-old data any time.
Okay. The dashboard tables refresh every fifteen minutes, and the finance tables stay nightly. We can revisit five minutes once Jun has measurements.
One more data question. Travel time between jobs is one of the dashboard charts. Do we copy the technicians' location breadcrumbs into the warehouse?
I'd rather not. The breadcrumbs are the most sensitive thing we hold. Every copy is one more place to delete them from.
Agreed. Our contracts promise customers that location history is purged on a schedule, and a warehouse copy makes that promise much harder to keep.
Then we compute travel time per job in production and copy only that number. No raw breadcrumbs in the warehouse at all.
That's easy. It's one extra column on the job when it's completed.
While we're on sensitive data, who inside Quillmark gets access to the new warehouse? Today half the company seems to have a Brindle login.
My team, Greta's team, and engineering on request. Everyone else gets dashboards, not raw tables.
And access through single sign-on only, so when someone leaves, their warehouse access goes with their account on the same day.
My team only needs the finance tables. They shouldn't be able to see customer job details at all, and they'd rather not.
Both vendors do permissions per schema, so that part is easy whichever one we pick.
Good. Least access by default: analytics, finance and engineering, through single sign-on, each limited to what they actually use.
Can we also use the migration to fix the naming? Half the Brindle tables have names nobody understands anymore.
Yes, but only where nothing depends on the old names. Renaming everything at once is how migrations miss their dates.
Please don't rename anything I reconcile against in December. New names for the new dashboard tables, and the finance tables stay as they are until after the close.
Good. Anselm, you said you had trial results on Quarrystone. Is now a good time?
Yes, and they change things, so it's good we didn't sign anything. I got further with the trial account yesterday afternoon.
First, row-level access. It exists, but only on their enterprise plan. On the plan I priced, there's no way to guarantee a customer only sees their own rows.
That's the one I was worried about. Without it, customer exports are off the table, or we build the filtering ourselves.
Second, and worse: on the standard plan, Quarrystone keeps backups in a Canadian region. Only enterprise lets you pin backups to the US.
That's a hard no. We tell every customer their data and backups stay in the US. Some of them have it written into their contracts.
And what does their enterprise plan cost? I assume it isn't a small step up from the one you priced.
I asked. For our volume it's about seventy thousand a year. So the cheap option stops being cheap the moment we need either of those two things.
Seventy thousand is more than Brindle. That's not a migration, that's a downgrade with extra steps.
And Fernhollow does both on its normal plan? Row-level access and US-only backups?
Both, on the standard plan. I checked their documentation and I asked their solutions engineer to confirm it in writing. He did, this morning.
Then let's reverse the lean. We go with Fernhollow, not Quarrystone. Backups outside the US are a non-starter, and row-level access only on their enterprise plan kills the price advantage.
Agreed. I'd rather pay more for the one that doesn't make us break promises to customers.
And two of my analysts have used Fernhollow at their last jobs. That shortens the learning curve more than any price difference would.
Their query language is close to what we write for Brindle today, too. Most report queries should move over with small edits, not rewrites.
And it's less of a gap than it looked. Their rep came back to me yesterday. On a two-year commitment they'll do forty three thousand dollars a year, instead of the fifty two thousand list price.
Forty three a year is a good deal less than the sixty one we pay Brindle, so the move pays for itself in the first year.
Good. Greta, are you comfortable committing to two years with a vendor we haven't used yet?
With an exit clause if they miss their uptime commitment, yes. I'll make sure that's in the paper before I sign it.
Before anyone signs, I'd like Odette to read their security documents. Backups, encryption, who on their side can get at the data.
Fine. If Odette's done by then, I'll sign the Fernhollow contract by Friday the sixteenth of October.
I'll ask her today. She's busy this week, but this one is mostly reading.
Okay. And Brindle. When exactly do we switch it off?
After the cutover, I'd keep it read-only for a couple of weeks, in case someone needs to compare a number with the old system.
But not past the renewal. If we're still on Brindle on the fifteenth of February, we're paying for another year.
Then Brindle gets switched off on Friday the twenty ninth of January. That's almost three weeks of read-only after the cutover, and still ahead of the renewal on the fifteenth of February.
And I need written notice to them by when? Let me check the contract. I think it's sixty days.
Yes, sixty days' notice before the renewal date. So the notice letter has to go out by the middle of December. I'll send it as soon as the parallel run starts.
What's the rollback if the cutover weekend goes badly? I'd like that written down before December, not invented on the night.
Brindle keeps getting the nightly copy until it's switched off. If Fernhollow has a bad weekend, every report points back at Brindle with one configuration change.
The dashboard would go back to day-old data during a rollback, which is annoying, but nothing actually breaks for anyone.
And the finance reports? I'd want those to be the very last thing to switch, not the first.
Then finance switches a day after everything else, on the Tuesday, once we've seen one clean night on Fernhollow.
Good. Rollback means pointing the reports back at Brindle, and finance switches last.
Does the forty three include the streaming, or is that metered on top? I've been burned by usage charges before.
Included, up to a volume we won't reach for a couple of years. I checked our growth against their tiers before the call.
Good. Owners. Anselm, you lead the whole migration?
Yes. I'll own the Fernhollow setup, the change stream, the backfill and the cutover weekend itself.
I'll re-point the dispatcher dashboard at Fernhollow. That's my team's code, so it should be quick once the tables exist.
And I can do the finance reports as well. There are twelve of them. They're mostly copies of Brindle queries anyway.
I'd rather you didn't. No offence, Mirela, but those twelve reports are what I sign the year with, and I know every quirk in them.
I'll rebuild the twelve finance reports in Fernhollow myself, by Friday the eighteenth of December, so they run in the parallel run alongside the Brindle versions.
No offence taken. That frees me up for the dashboard and the customer exports, which are the parts my team is actually excited about.
And I'll set up the replica lag alert before the fourteenth of December, so we know about trouble before the dispatchers do.
One more thing on the holidays. The parallel run covers the last two weeks of December. Who watches the comparison job when everyone's away?
I'm around for most of it. I'll take the first week, and I'd like someone from Jun's team on the second.
I'll find someone. Engineering already has a rotation covering that week, so it can go on the same schedule.
Customer exports. Do they come in this migration, or after it?
After. The migration is already a lot. Exports come once we've had a month on Fernhollow without surprises.
Agreed, exports are a follow-up, not part of the cutover.
One request for the project plan: put the Brindle notice date and the switch-off date on it in red. Those are the two dates that cost money if we miss them.
Will do. And I'll put the cutover weekend on everyone's calendar now, so nobody books a holiday over it by accident.
Put the Tuesday finance switch on there as well, so Greta's team knows exactly when their reports change underneath them.
Okay, let me recap so the notes are right.

Fernhollow at forty three thousand a year on two years, Greta signs by the sixteenth of October. Parallel run from the fourteenth of December, cutover on the eleventh of January, Brindle off on the twenty ninth.

Three years of history in the warehouse, the rest archived. Dashboard tables every fifteen minutes, finance nightly, no raw breadcrumbs. Anselm leads, Mirela does the dashboard, Greta the finance reports.
That matches my notes. I'll turn it into a project plan with the dates and send it round tomorrow.
And I'll want a single page showing the Brindle and Fernhollow costs side by side, for the budget file.
I'll add that as the first page. Thanks, everyone, that was a lot more decisive than I expected going in.

items.text: Choose Fernhollow over Quarrystone for the new warehouse: Quarrystone keeps backups outside the US and has row-level access only on its enterprise plan (reverses the earlier lean)
Fernhollow: $43,000 a year on a two-year commitment (list price $52,000); Brindle costs $61,000 a year
Cutover moves from Monday November 30 to Monday January 11, after year-end close; four-week parallel run from December 14
Load three years of job history into the warehouse; older data goes to archive files in cold storage, kept seven years
Dashboard tables refresh every 15 minutes; finance tables stay nightly; no raw location breadcrumbs in the warehouse
Switch Brindle off on Friday January 29, before its February 15 renewal
Rebuild the twelve finance reports in Fernhollow by Friday December 18
Sign the Fernhollow contract by Friday October 16, after Odette's review of their security documents
Set up a replica lag alert before December 14
